growth_story.headline: After civil war and political turmoil stalled it for 17 years, Guinea-Bissau's income per person has grown steadily since 2015, with cashew at the center.
growth_story.arc: Guinea-Bissau's income per person grew 2.5 percent a year from 1990 to 1997, then stalled for 17 years, averaging -0.1 percent a year from 1998 to 2014. That era opened with a civil war in 1998–99, when income per person fell 23.9 percent in a single year, and went on through frequent changes of government and the killing of senior officials, including the president in 2009. Politics calmed somewhat after 2015, donor money revived public investment, and growth returned to 2.5 percent a year from 2015 to 2025. Cashew is the backbone of the economy and its main export, so the size of the harvest and the world cashew price move growth from year to year. Income per person reached a new high in 2025, but it only passed its 1997 level again in 2016, nearly two decades after the war.

threads.title: Civil war and coups
threads.text: A short civil war in 1998–99 cut income per person by 23.9 percent in 1998, and a partial rebound of 14.6 percent in 1999 did not undo it. Coups, coup attempts, killings of senior officials and frequent changes of government kept politics unstable for years afterward, and growth averaged -0.1 percent a year from 1998 to 2014.

threads.title: Turbulence, then calmer politics
threads.text: Public investment fell during the turbulent years from 2008 to 2013, and income per person dropped 4.3 percent in 2012. After 2015 politics steadied a little, a president served a full term for the first time, and donor money revived public investment as growth picked up.

threads.title: An economy built on cashew
threads.text: Cashew is the main export and a large part of the economy, so good harvests and high prices lift growth and poor ones hold it back. A bigger crop and better prices drove the 2025 upswing, when income per person grew 3.6 percent.

threads.title: More jobs, not more output
threads.text: Most rural adults work, but fewer than one in ten holds a wage job. A 2026 World Bank survey of firms finds them hiring more workers without producing more.

threads.title: Instability returns in 2025
threads.text: The military took over the government in November 2025, days after elections, a return of the kind of upheaval that marked the stalled era. The sources report calm since then, but they expect the uncertainty to weigh on investment in 2026.

since_last_year.text: Income per person grew 3.6 percent in 2025, its fastest pace since 2011, on a large cashew harvest and higher cashew prices. After elections in November 2025 the military took over the government, and the World Bank now expects growth to ease in 2026 as investment slows amid political uncertainty, with new elections planned for December 2026.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe brisk growth in 2025, but income per person in the data rose a smaller 3.6 percent, because a fast-growing population takes a large share of the gains. The World Bank's 2023 diagnostic also calls growth low and volatile, yet in the data income per person has grown every year since 2015, averaging 2.4 percent a year over 2016–2025 against 0.8 in the decade before.
